passage:
"Noor, beti, Joseph uncle's family is coming at seven. Sit properly. No feet on the sofa."
"Can I show them my drawings?"
"Only if they ask. And don't interrupt the grown-ups."
"Is the chicken 65 for us?"
"Guests eat first. Then us."
At dinner, Noor sat very straight. She watched Joseph uncle take a third helping of chicken 65. Then his son took the last pieces. Noor's stomach growled. She said nothing, the way Mummy wanted.
After they left, Noor flopped on the sofa, feet up. "I didn't get even one piece!"
"I saw," Mummy said, sitting beside her. "You were so good tonight."
"Why do we act different when people come?"
Mummy thought. "Home has two faces, na. One for guests, one for us." She opened the fridge. "And this face kept some chicken aside for you."
Noor squealed.

qa.q: What time was Joseph uncle's family coming?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: How did Noor feel watching Joseph uncle's son take the last pieces?
qa.a: She felt resentful and hungry, her stomach growling, but kept quiet as Mummy wanted.

qa.q: What did Mummy do after the guests left that helped?
qa.a: She praised Noor's effort, explained that home has a face for guests and one for the family, and showed she had saved chicken for her.

qa.q: How might Joseph uncle's family have seen the evening?
qa.a: They probably felt warmly welcomed and well fed, with no idea that Noor had missed her favourite dish.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to behave well and let guests eat first, who resents missing a favourite dish and learns home has a public and a private face.

passage:
It's a few months ago now, but I still remember that Sunday. I, Ayesha, was the only daughter at home, sitting at the dining table with my chemistry book spread out, two days before the board exam. The doorbell rang. Six relatives from Aligarh, unannounced. Ammi called, "Ayesha, chai banao, jaldi." My brother Wasim was lying on the sofa playing a phone game. Nobody called him.
I made tea, then pakoras, then more tea. Two hours. My notes lay untouched. Every time I passed the sofa, Wasim was still playing. I smiled at the guests and felt boiling inside.
That night I didn't shout. I told Ammi quietly, "I love serving guests. But Wasim can boil water too. Especially in exam week." Ammi was silent a long time. Then she said, "You're right." Now when guests come, Wasim carries the tray. He spills a little. That's fine.

qa.q: What was Wasim doing while Ayesha served the guests?
qa.a: He was lying on the sofa playing a phone game.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel while serving the guests during exam week?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful, boiling inside while smiling at the guests, because her study time was taken and her brother was left alone.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha's approach that night work?
qa.a: She spoke quietly and fairly, honouring guests while asking that her brother share the serving, which let Ammi see the unfairness.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen the situation before Ayesha spoke?
qa.a: Ammi probably called her daughter out of habit, without noticing that Wasim was never asked or that exams were close.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager pulled from study to serve relatives while her brother is left alone, and how fairness in who serves matters.

passage:
Sonali, twenty-one, had three exams that week and a one-room flat in Siliguri. On Monday night the bell rang: Pema aunty, her mother's cousin, with two big bags and a smile. "I came for my knee doctor! I'll stay with you, na?" Sonali smiled back and made up the spare mattress. By Wednesday aunty was still there, watching serials loudly while Sonali tried to revise with cotton in her ears. Nobody had said how long. Sonali kept smiling and kept wondering: a week? A month? Saying no to family felt impossible.
On Wednesday night she made two cups of tea and sat beside aunty. "Aunty, I love having you. But I have exams till Friday, and I'm scared I'll fail. When is your next appointment?" Pema aunty looked surprised, then embarrassed. "Oh beta, I didn't think. Friday afternoon." She turned the TV down, and on Thursday she cooked dinner while Sonali studied.

qa.q: When was Pema aunty's next appointment?
qa.a: Friday afternoon.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling while she kept smiling at Pema aunty?
qa.a: She felt anxious and trapped, worried about her exams but finding it impossible to say no to family.

qa.q: What made Sonali's conversation work?
qa.a: She spoke warmly, said she loved having aunty, explained her exams honestly and asked about timing, which protected both the relationship and her studies.

qa.q: How might Pema aunty have felt when Sonali explained about her exams?
qa.a: She felt surprised and embarrassed at not having thought of it, then caring, turning the TV down and cooking dinner.

grounding: It illustrates a host who smiles while wondering how long a relative will stay, and uses gentle honest talk about timing.

passage:
"Sachin, what's in the box?"
"Just some sweets for your mother, Mohit. From the shop near my hostel."
"You didn't have to."
"My Nani would kill me if I came empty-handed."
Mohit's mother opened the door. "Arre, Sachin! Come, come."
"Namaste, aunty. These are for you."
After lunch, Sachin stood up and began stacking plates.
"Beta, sit, you're a guest!"
"Please, aunty, let me at least carry them to the kitchen."
She laughed and let him. In the kitchen he dried the dishes while she washed.
At four, Mohit's father yawned for the third time.
Sachin picked up his bag. "Uncle, aunty, thank you. That was the best rajma I've had since I left home."
"Stay for tea!"
"Next time, aunty. You've already fed me like a king."
At the gate, Mohit said, "My mother's going to compare every friend to you now."

qa.q: What did Sachin bring for Mohit's mother?
qa.a: Sweets from the shop near Sachin's hostel.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Mohit's father yawned for the third time?
qa.a: Sachin probably felt thoughtful and a little concerned, sensing the hosts were tired and it was time to leave.

qa.q: What made Sachin a good guest?
qa.a: He brought a small gift, helped in the kitchen, thanked his hosts warmly and left before they were too tired.

qa.q: How does Mohit's mother see Sachin?
qa.a: She sees him as a warm, well-mannered guest, so much that Mohit thinks she will compare every friend to him.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who brings a small gift, helps in the kitchen and leaves before the hosts are tired.

passage:
Mohit, you asked why I stopped doing big dinners, so here's the real story, from me, Vandana. Last year my husband's relatives came from Nagpur for a week. I wanted everything perfect. I didn't want his aunt saying we live small. So I ordered from the expensive caterer, bought new curtains, took them to a fancy restaurant twice. I put it all on the credit card. I smiled the whole week. Inside I was sick with worry. After they left, the bill came, and I cried in the bathroom. It took us months to sort it out with the bank.
And do you know what his aunt remembered? Not the curtains. She said, "Your aloo parathas on the last morning, with that green chutney. Just like my mother's." That was the cheapest meal of the week. Now I cook simple food, set the table nicely and sit down with my guests. Nobody has complained.

qa.q: What meal did the aunt remember?
qa.a: The aloo parathas on the last morning, with the green chutney.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel during the week of the visit?
qa.a: Vandana felt anxious and afraid of being judged, smiling outside but sick with worry inside.

qa.q: What did Vandana change, and why is it still real hospitality?
qa.a: Vandana now cooks simple food, sets the table nicely and sits with the guests; the warmth and time spent together are what guests actually remember.

qa.q: How might the aunt have felt about the visit?
qa.a: The aunt seemed warmly touched by the simple parathas, which reminded her of her mother, more than impressed by the expensive things.

grounding: It illustrates a host who spends beyond her means to avoid looking poor, and learns a warm simple welcome is real hospitality.

passage:
"Noor, did I do something wrong? Pieter left hungry."
"What happened, Eshaan?"
"I asked if he wanted more biryani. He said, 'No, thank you.' So I said, 'Arre, have a little.' He said no again. Then I put some on his plate anyway, like my mother does."
"And?"
"He looked really uncomfortable. He didn't eat it."
Noor laughed softly. "In your mother's house, a guest says no twice to be polite, and the host insists. Here in Amsterdam, no means no."
"So I was forcing food on him?"
"A bit, yes. And your aunt last month in Lucknow, remember? I said 'no, thank you' once and she never offered again. I went to bed hungry."
Eshaan groaned. "So it's the opposite for each of us."
"Exactly. Ask once here. Ask three times in Lucknow."
"I'll message Pieter tomorrow. And save him some biryani."

qa.q: What did Eshaan do after Pieter said no twice?
qa.a: Eshaan put some on Pieter's plate anyway, like Eshaan's mother does.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when the polite no in Lucknow was taken as final?
qa.a: Noor probably felt embarrassed and a bit awkward, too polite to ask again and going to bed hungry.

qa.q: What rule does Noor suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Ask once in Amsterdam and three times in Lucknow; knowing the local rule avoids both offence and awkwardness.

qa.q: How did Pieter probably experience the extra biryani?
qa.a: Pieter probably felt uncomfortable and pressured, since for him a first no was final, so he left it uneaten.

grounding: It illustrates a young person noticing that some cultures expect insisting and refusing twice while others take a first no as final.

passage:
Daycare note, Wednesday lunch.
Uma grabbed rice with her whole fist and pushed some into Payal's mouth. Payal opened wide and laughed. Then Uma reached into my plate for a piece of carrot and held it up to my lips. When I took it, she clapped. She wanted a bite from everyone's plate and offered her own soggy roti round the table. I let the girls share, wiped hands after, and told Uma's mother how generous she is.

qa.q: What did Uma push into Payal's mouth?
qa.a: Rice, with her whole fist.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when the carer took the carrot?
qa.a: She felt delighted, clapping happily.

qa.q: What did the carer do that suited Uma's age?
qa.a: Let the children share food freely as a way of bonding, and simply wiped hands afterwards.

qa.q: How did Payal seem to experience being fed by Uma?
qa.a: Payal seemed happy and amused, opening wide and laughing.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler who shares food from her own hand and expects bites from everyone's plate, with no sense of clean or unclean.

passage: At the London park, Pablo held out his juice bottle to Tariq. "Want some?" Tariq, five, shook his head hard. "No! Jootha!" Pablo frowned. "What's jootha?" Tariq didn't know exactly. Nani said it about glasses you already drank from. "It's... not allowed." Pablo looked sad and put the bottle away. Tariq felt bad. At home he asked Nani why. She poured juice into two paper cups. "Now you can share." Next day, Tariq brought two cups.

qa.q: What did Tariq bring the next day?
qa.a: Two cups.

qa.q: How did Tariq feel after Pablo put the bottle away?
qa.a: He felt bad and a bit confused, following Nani's rule without really understanding it.

qa.q: How did Nani help Tariq keep the rule and still share?
qa.a: She poured juice into two separate cups, showing a way to share without drinking from one bottle.

qa.q: How might Pablo have felt when Tariq shouted "Jootha"?
qa.a: Pablo probably felt confused and hurt, not knowing why his friend refused.

grounding: It illustrates a child who follows a rule about not drinking from another's glass before understanding why.

passage:
"Kavitha, why do you have two sets of plates?"
"Those are for Ammamma. She doesn't eat from plates that had eggs."
Anjali looked around the kitchen. "No eggs at all?"
"Not in this kitchen. Appa eats omelettes at the canteen."
"At my house we have eggs every morning. And fish on Sundays."
"Really? Fish?" Kavitha wrinkled her nose, then laughed. "Sorry. Is it nice?"
"Very nice. Is Ammamma angry if I bring my egg sandwich?"
"Hmm. Maybe eat it on the balcony? Then it's not in the kitchen."
"Okay." Anjali thought. "Can I try your Ammamma's sambar?"
Kavitha's grandmother, listening from the door, smiled and filled a small bowl. "Ask me anything, kanna. Better than guessing."
Anjali tasted it. "Can you teach my mum?"

qa.q: Why does Kavitha's house have two sets of plates?
qa.a: Because Ammamma doesn't eat from plates that had eggs.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as she looked around the kitchen?
qa.a: Anjali felt curious and a little surprised, noticing rules very different from her own home.

qa.q: How did Anjali and Kavitha keep the friendship open?
qa.a: They asked each other kindly about eggs and fish instead of mocking, and found an easy solution like eating on the balcony.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's grandmother feel about Anjali's questions?
qa.a: She seems pleased and warm, smiling and inviting Anjali to ask rather than guess.

grounding: It illustrates a child noticing a friend's home has different kitchen rules and asking kindly rather than mocking.

passage:
Suraj, your mother says you won't take your fish tiffin to school anymore. Let your Sharmila bua tell you something. When I was fourteen, at the convent school in Mumbai, Aai packed me bombil fry, dried fish, every Monday. The first time I opened it, a girl held her nose and said, "Chee, who died?" The whole row laughed. I shut the box and went hungry. For months I threw it in the dustbin and ate biscuits. I was so ashamed of my own home.
Then one day a new girl, Farzana, sat next to me. She smelled it and said, "Is that bombil? My Nani makes it! Please, one piece." I gave her one. Then she brought her Nani's kebabs to share. By the end of term, half the class wanted my Monday tiffin. I learnt: the food didn't change. Only who was sitting next to me.

qa.q: What did Sharmila's Aai pack every Monday?
qa.a: Bombil fry, dried fish.

qa.q: How did young Sharmila feel after the girl said "Chee, who died?"
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed of her own home food, shutting the box and going hungry.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what does it show?
qa.a: Farzana asking for a piece of bombil; it shows how one peer's warm response can turn food shame into pride.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt when she smelled the bombil?
qa.a: Farzana probably felt happy and at home, reminded of her Nani's cooking.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager embarrassed by a smelly home lunch until a peer's delight turns shame into pride.
